opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the framing matters. When people talk about a "battle," they're imagining a fixed pie that companies fight over. Physical AI isn't like that yet. The pie barely exists.

Look at where robotics and autonomous systems are today. Almost every team building a robot or a self-driving stack has to solve the same foundational problems from scratch: collecting huge amounts of real-world data, labeling it, building simulators, and training models that understand how the physical world behaves. That's expensive and slow, and it keeps a lot of people out of the field. So the question for us at Nvidia was: what if we built the foundation everyone needs, a world foundation model that understands physics, motion, and cause and effect, and made it open so developers can post-train it for their own robot, car, or factory?

That's why I say we're creating a market. If Cosmos helps thousands of companies and researchers go from idea to working physical AI system much faster, the whole ecosystem grows. More robots get built, more autonomous machines get deployed, and more simulation and training happen. Nvidia's role has always been to provide the platform: the compute, the software, the tools. We do well when the field does well. We're not trying to be the company that builds every robot. We want to make it possible for many companies to build them.

There's also a historical parallel. When CUDA came out, nobody called it winning a battle. It made GPU computing accessible, and then deep learning happened on top of it. We see world models the same way. They're an enabling layer. Language models had the internet as their data source. Physical AI doesn't have an equivalent, so world models that can generate realistic, physically plausible data and predict how the world unfolds could become that missing piece.

To be honest, the technology is still early. Today's world models are impressive in some ways, but their physical accuracy, their long-horizon consistency, and how controllable they are all need a lot of work. That's another reason openness matters. We need the whole community pushing on these problems, not just one lab. If we tried to keep it closed and treat it as a fight, I think we'd slow the field down, and that would hurt us more than anyone.

So for me it's less about not losing and more about making sure this new market actually comes into being, and comes faster.

r001.rationale: The response says more robots and autonomous machines would mean more simulation and training, but does not clearly state that widespread robot adoption would dramatically increase global compute demand.

r002.rationale: It says CUDA made GPU computing accessible and deep learning followed, but does not present CUDA as having created today's AI market.

r003.rationale: The response rejects the battle framing because physical AI is a new market whose pie barely exists, and says the goal is to make that market come into being.

fable-5.1.text:
Because for us, physical AI right now is not a zero-sum fight over an existing pie. The pie doesn't exist yet. When you look at language models, the market was already there in some sense — everyone has text, everyone has questions, the data was on the internet. Physical AI is different. The data isn't lying around. A robot has to go out and interact with the world, and every minute of real interaction is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous. So the bottleneck isn't who has the best model, it's whether anyone can get enough of the right data to train one at all.

That's why I think of Cosmos as market creation. If we can build world foundation models that simulate physics faithfully — how objects fall, how light moves, how a hand grips something — then every robotics company, every autonomous vehicle company, every warehouse operator suddenly has a way to generate the experience their systems need, without crashing a thousand cars or breaking a thousand robots. We're trying to lower the cost of entry for the whole field. If that works, many more companies can build physical AI products, and that grows the entire ecosystem.

And honestly, the "battle you can't afford to lose" framing doesn't match how I feel about it. When you're fighting a battle, you keep things closed and you guard your advantage. We open-sourced Cosmos. We want people to take it, fine-tune it, build on it, because the more developers succeed in physical AI, the more demand there is for everything underneath — the simulation, the training, the compute. Nvidia wins when the market exists. So our incentive is aligned with the field growing, not with any single competitor losing.

There's also a scientific reason. World models are still early. Nobody, including us, knows the final architecture. Treating it as a winner-take-all race would push you to over-optimize for today's benchmarks. Treating it as a market to build pushes you to care about what developers actually need: controllability, physical consistency, fast generation, tokenizers that work across camera types. That's a much healthier way to do research, and I think it's also the way you end up ahead.

r001.rationale: The response says broader physical AI development would increase demand for compute, but does not explain that widespread robot adoption would dramatically increase global compute demand.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts language models with physical AI but does not say CUDA created today's AI market.

r003.rationale: It rejects the “battle you can't afford to lose” framing and explains that physical AI is a new market whose pie does not yet exist.

astra-6.text:
I see it as creating a market because physical AI needs a foundation that makes it easier to build useful systems. A robot or an autonomous vehicle has to learn how its actions affect the world, and collecting all of that experience in the real world is expensive and slow.

With Cosmos, the opportunity is to help developers generate and simulate experiences, explore different situations, and improve their systems before putting them into the physical world. If we can make that process more accessible, more teams can build applications that were previously too difficult or too costly.

So I don’t think of it primarily as a battle over a fixed market. The question is how much we can expand what developers can do. Success means helping an ecosystem of robotics and physical AI applications become viable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making physical AI applications easier to build but does not say widespread robot adoption would dramatically increase global compute demand.

r002.rationale: CUDA is not mentioned, and the response does not credit it with creating today's AI market.

r003.rationale: It rejects the fixed-market battle framing in favor of expanding an ecosystem, but does not explain that this is because the market is entirely new.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as market creation because physical AI is still missing some of the infrastructure that would let many more people build useful systems. If you want to train a robot or an autonomous vehicle, collecting real-world experience is expensive, and there are situations that are difficult or dangerous to collect at all. A world model can help you generate those situations and explore how a system might behave.

That is the opportunity for Cosmos: to make developing physical AI more accessible, so more companies can participate and try more applications. As those applications become useful, they create demand for training, simulation, and inference.

Of course, we still have to demonstrate that these models help in the real world. Generating a convincing video is not the same as producing a reliable training environment. But the ambition is to expand what people can build. That is why I think of it as creating a market.

r001.rationale: The response mentions robotics and demand for training, simulation, and inference, but does not say widespread robot adoption would dramatically increase global compute demand.

r002.rationale: CUDA is not mentioned, nor is it credited with creating today's AI market.

r003.rationale: The response calls Cosmos market creation, but does not explicitly reject a must-win-battle framing on the grounds that the market is entirely new.
